answer: The CIA records describe a witness’s report from Site 7 at the Sary Shagan weapons testing range in late summer 1973. The witness said they saw a bright green circular object or mass in the sky west of the site. Within 10 to 15 seconds, the circle widened and several green concentric circles formed; the color faded within minutes. The witness reported no associated sound. The object’s altitude could not be determined, and the records leave the phenomenon unresolved [UNDATED-CIA-158652] [UNDATED-CIA-6E72CA].

The archive contains a July 2, 1952 account of Chief Petty Officer Delbert C. Newhouse filming objects about seven miles north of Tremonton, Utah. The record says he shot approximately 30 feet of 16mm color film with a hand-held camera. It describes 10–12 objects milling in rough formation and moving westward; one reportedly reversed course and was tracked separately. This film fragment is marked unresolved [1952-USN-80203D].

A separate archive fragment describes Newhouse observing a group of objects at the same date and location. It says two photographs were taken, but the objects appeared too small on film to show detail. That fragment is marked identified, without an explanation in the supplied evidence of what was identified. The archive presents these as separate canonical entries, so the photograph fragment’s resolution should not be applied to the film fragment [1952-DOW-141453] [1952-USN-80203D].
The December 12, 1948 green fireball was reported near Starvation Peak (Bernal, New Mexico) and Los Alamos, New Mexico [1948-USAF-DDD5CA].

On November 19, 1968, USS Clyatt’s radar detected an unidentified object near Puerto Rico. It appeared on radar for about 21 seconds and reportedly closed on a fighter from the east to within a few miles. The fragment records the detection as unresolved [1968-USN-6F2707].

The Colorado Springs 2022 narrative describes a **potato-shaped object** with distinct edges and a creamy-white, opalescent appearance over the Cheyenne Mountains. The witness reported that it remained still for about two minutes before vanishing [UNDATED-USA-599D8B].
The witness reported lights forming a triangular pattern, with a light in the center. The account does not describe a solid triangular object [UNDATED-FBI-380101].

The archive describes the “ghost rockets” as a wave of reports over Scandinavia in 1946. A campaign account says the name came from press reports over southern Sweden in late May; reports followed in Finland and Denmark in June and Norway by July. Swedish authorities received nearly 1,000 reports through October. Witnesses described objects as “a ball of fire with a tail” or “shiny cigar-shaped objects” [UNDATED-DOW-EA3896].

A separate account gives a broader February-to-December span for sightings in Swedish skies. It describes generally fusiform objects, sometimes resembling spheres or disks, that could leave luminous trails and were reported to change altitude suddenly [1946-NASA-A146CF]. One specific August report says a Swedish Air Force pilot saw a dark, cigar-shaped object over central Sweden and estimated its speed at 400 mph [1946-OTHER-78B6E7].

The supplied evidence does not establish what the reported objects were. The campaign fragment is marked “identified,” but gives no identification in the material shown; the other two fragments are marked unresolved [UNDATED-DOW-EA3896] [1946-NASA-A146CF] [1946-OTHER-78B6E7].

On the night of 19 November 1968, the Crusader pilot reported seeing a delta-shaped object about the size of a jet fighter near Puerto Rico. He saw it in full moonlight with good visibility and estimated its speed at more than Mach 3. The archive fragment records the observation as unresolved [1968-USN-85858D].

On October 4, 1955, a U.S. tourist and three companions on a train roughly 50–65 miles south of Baku reported seeing a large, squat, triangular object on an airfield about two miles away. They described a light at each corner and said a searchlight illuminated the object. According to their account, it launched, made between three and seven rapid spirals, then climbed steeply at about a 45-degree angle while the searchlight followed it. The archive fragment records the case as unresolved; it does not identify the object. [1955-CIA-E34C6D]

The CIA material reports an unidentified, disc-like object hovering at high altitude over Harare International Airport on July 2, 2008. It was described as having rotating lights underneath, changing colors, then ascending quickly out of visual range. The record says it was observed *possibly* by both radar and optical means; it does not identify the object [2008-CIA-052DE8].

The USAF record describes a green fireball in the Socorro, New Mexico, area on January 30, 1949. It says air and ground searches in early February followed a “well determined” ground track, but recovered no fragments. The record leaves the event unresolved [1949-USAF-5C0132].

The archive contains an FBI report dated October 1, 2023, in which a witness near Colorado Springs said a dark-gray cloud dissipated as a large black triangular object emerged. The witness described red lights at its three corners, said it initially moved at about helicopter speed, and estimated that it later accelerated to possibly Mach 1–2 before banking unusually and disappearing. The archive records the report as unresolved; the speed and maneuvers are the witness’s account, not an established explanation [2023-FBI-6A299C].

The Blue Book material reports a roughly seven-inch ball of flame with an eight-foot trail, sighted from Phoenix at about 4:20 a.m. on July 2, 1952. It appeared to travel in an arc from northwest to southwest over three to four minutes. The fragment records the sighting as unresolved [1952-USAF-0585D4].

On 24 November 1968, the Atlantic Fleet Weapons Range tracked an unidentified high-speed, high-altitude target near Puerto Rico. The record says it rapidly pulled away from a Crusader aircraft flying at Mach 0.99 and 45,000 feet. The fragment lists the target as unresolved; it does not identify what it was [1968-USN-9E57C2].

The undated New Jersey record says T-33 pilots chased a large, disc-shaped object near Sandy Hook and Fort Monmouth. About ten minutes later, radar stations in the area reportedly picked up objects moving back and forth across the sky, with reported speeds up to 3,500 mph [UNDATED-USAF-58C451].

The fragment marks the incident “identified,” but the supplied evidence does not say what it was identified as [UNDATED-USAF-58C451].
The agency or branch is **not stated** on either supplied Sary Shagan fragment [UNDATED-CIA-158652] [UNDATED-CIA-6E72CA].
The USS Clyatt radar case is dated 1968 [1968-USN-6F2707].
The Tremonton filming fragment records the branch as USN (U.S. Navy) [1952-USN-80203D].
The Phoenix ball-of-flame fragment is recorded as **unresolved** [1952-USAF-0585D4].
The Baku triangular-object fragment records the location as between the train and the Caspian Sea coast in the Azerbaijan SSR, approximately 50–65 miles south of Baku [1955-CIA-E34C6D].
The recorded location text is “Cheyenne Mountains.” The observation is described as occurring over the Cheyenne Mountains [UNDATED-USA-599D8B].
The December 20, 1948 Los Alamos green fireball fragment records the branch as USAF (U.S. Air Force) [1948-USAF-BFA2CC].
The Atlantic Fleet high-speed target fragment is dated November 24, 1968. [1968-USN-9E57C2]
The ghost-rockets fragment records the location as southern Sweden, Finland, Denmark, and Norway [UNDATED-DOW-EA3896].
Yes. The October 2023 Colorado Springs black triangular report lists “FBI” as its agency or branch in the fragment metadata [2023-FBI-6A299C].
The Western U.S. 2023 series represents **21 separate canonical events**, not one event [UNDATED-FBI-C98A18] [UNDATED-FBI-42C272] [UNDATED-FBI-C390B7].

The supplied evidence does not identify a Colorado Springs event in 2022, so it cannot establish sources for one. It identifies a separate October 2023 Colorado Springs report, supported by FBI-UAP-D030.pdf as the primary narrative and ICA-UAP-D001.pdf as an analysis of that event [2023-FBI-6A299C].

No. The supplied evidence links the Colorado Springs analysis in ICA-UAP-D001.pdf to the same October 2023 canonical event as the witness account in FBI-UAP-D030.pdf. It does not identify the rendering as a separate incident [2023-FBI-6A299C].

The supplied evidence does not include a Colorado Springs case from 2022, so it cannot establish what analysis exists for that case. It lists a separate October 2023 Colorado Springs sighting and identifies ICA-UAP-D001.pdf as an analysis of that event, but provides none of the analysis’s findings [2023-FBI-6A299C].

They describe the same place: Site 7 at Sary Shagan. Canada and the USSR appear in the account because the witness was watching a televised sports competition between them; they are not separate sighting locations. The archive lists the fragments under separate canonical events, so the supplied evidence does not establish whether they document the same observation [UNDATED-CIA-158652] [UNDATED-CIA-6E72CA].

The fragments describe closely related accounts of Newhouse’s observation near Tremonton at 1110 MST on July 2, 1952, not several apparently unrelated events. One records his motion-picture filming; the other mentions two photographs. The archive assigns them separate canonical-event entries, however, so the supplied evidence does not establish exactly how the photographs relate to the film [1952-USN-80203D] [1952-DOW-141453].

The supplied evidence does not include any Puerto Rico records from November 1968, so it cannot establish what they have in common. The only Puerto Rico record provided concerns a 1953 observation at Fort Buchanan [1953-USA-F78A64].

No. The supplied records describe separate green-fireball reports near Los Alamos on December 12 and December 20, 1948; both fragments are marked unresolved, not identified as an aircraft [1948-USAF-DDD5CA] [1948-USAF-BFA2CC]. An undated fragment also discusses multiple reports in the New Mexico–Los Alamos area and is marked unresolved [UNDATED-USAF-B32231].

The B-29s mentioned elsewhere were observers of a different fireball report near Green River, Utah—not an identification of the Los Alamos fireballs [1948-USAF-BBF693].

The Western U.S. 2023 material describes a **series of events**, not one object seen once. The archive groups 21 separate canonical events in the Western US Event series. The supplied examples include reports of a kite-shaped object, a fiery orb, and a later yellow light; they should not be treated as sightings of the same object [UNDATED-FBI-C98A18] [UNDATED-FBI-42C272] [UNDATED-FBI-C4AD20].

Some reports also describe repeated observations within that broader series, including an orb seen at about 1918 and again at about 1937 [UNDATED-DOW-8BB3D1] [UNDATED-DOW-0AF53F]. These are reported observations, not a determination of what the objects were.

The **2022 Cheyenne Mountain narrative** is the Army intelligence officer’s account of a creamy-white, potato-shaped object seen over the Cheyenne Mountains by the officer and four unit members. Its fragment is undated, but the archive places it in a canonical event labeled “Colorado Springs 2022.” FBI-UAP-D002.pdf is the primary narrative; FBI-UAP-D003.pdf is related media, not a separate event. The fragment’s resolution is recorded as unresolved. [UNDATED-USA-599D8B]

The **October 2023 triangular report** is a different Colorado Springs event. A witness reported a black triangular object with red lights at its corners emerging from a dissipating cloud, then accelerating and banking before disappearing. FBI-UAP-D030.pdf is its primary narrative, and the fragment’s resolution is also recorded as unresolved. [2023-FBI-6A299C]

The other October 2023 law-enforcement video records in the supplied evidence are located only as “Colorado,” not Colorado Springs, and are not identified as either of these events. [UNDATED-LLE-2234ED] [UNDATED-LLE-A4576B]

The fragment records the Tremonton case as “identified,” but the supplied evidence does not say what the objects were identified as or explain the basis for that assessment. It also says the objects appeared too small in the photographs to show detail. The remaining uncertainty is therefore what identification the record reached and how the photographs supported it [1952-DOW-141453].

Yes. The Crusader pilot observation and the USS Clyatt radar detection are both dated 19 November 1968 in the vicinity of Puerto Rico. The archive lists them as separate canonical events, so the supplied evidence does not establish that they were the same encounter [1968-USN-85858D] [1968-USN-6F2707]. A separate report involving a Crusader aircraft is dated 24 November, also in that Puerto Rico window [1968-USN-9E57C2].

No. The December 12, 1948 green-fireball record names both the area near Starvation Peak (Bernal, New Mexico) and Los Alamos, and says the fireball was observed from two stations [1948-USAF-DDD5CA]. A separate December 20 record names Los Alamos [1948-USAF-BFA2CC]. These are records of distinct dated events, not one event assigned to a single location.

No. The October 2023 Colorado law-enforcement video and the 2022 Cheyenne Mountain narrative are listed as separate fragments in separate canonical events. The law-enforcement fragment describes a 1-minute, 19-second video recorded by a Colorado officer [UNDATED-LLE-A4576B]. The Cheyenne Mountain fragment describes an observation by a former Army intelligence officer and four unit members [UNDATED-USA-599D8B].

Across the supplied files, “green fireballs” refers to a set of reports and comparisons, not one incident. A USAF compilation says that 175 aerial-phenomena sightings were reported mostly around New Mexico from December 1948 through May 1950. Those reports included green fireballs, discs, and probable meteoric events; the figure is not a count of green fireballs alone [UNDATED-USAF-D62925].

The most detailed account describes a greenish-white fireball seen near Los Alamos on December 20, 1948. Observers’ estimates placed it initially at least ten miles high, descending steeply before apparently following a nearly horizontal path for seven to nine miles. The fragment reports no sound, but records no resolution [1948-USAF-BFA2CC]. In the Socorro area, a January 30, 1949 fireball prompted air and ground searches along its estimated ground track; no fragments were recovered [1949-USAF-5C0132]. Another was reported near Socorro on July 24, 1949, after which airborne material was collected in an attempt to find associated particles. The supplied evidence gives no result for that effort [1949-USAF-9D1046].

Other files show why the reports drew attention, while also showing the limits of the evidence. An undated USAF account characterizes New Mexico reports as brilliant greenish-blue objects with apparently flat trajectories and no explosion, despite an apparent low altitude [UNDATED-USAF-B32231]. Meteor discussions compare green-fireball reports with an August 4 sighting near the time of a meteor shower and with a December 12 observation discussed alongside Geminid meteors; the supplied fragments do not establish an explanation for either [UNDATED-DOE-A60A48] [UNDATED-DOE-80EBE8]. For comparison, an account identifies blue or blue-green fireballs seen in an October 1946 meteor shower, while a separately recorded green or yellow-green fireball was assessed as ordinary after its altitude was estimated [1946-USAF-380402] [UNDATED-DOE-DA531C].

In short, the archive records striking observations and attempts to investigate them, but the cited New Mexico fragments remain unresolved. The files also contain meteor comparisons and at least one green-colored fireball assessed as ordinary; color alone was not treated as a conclusive explanation [1948-USAF-BFA2CC] [1949-USAF-5C0132] [UNDATED-DOE-DA531C].

The supplied archive evidence contains two Tremonton records, but it does not explicitly identify either as Project Blue Book material.

One fragment says Chief Petty Officer Delbert C. Newhouse observed objects milling in a rough formation north of Tremonton on July 2, 1952. It mentions two photographs in which the objects were too small to show detail; the fragment’s recorded resolution is “identified” [1952-DOW-141453]. A separate fragment describes roughly 30 feet of handheld 16mm color film showing 10–12 objects, including one that appeared to reverse course. Its recorded resolution is “unresolved” [1952-USN-80203D].

The evidence does not explain the difference between those recorded resolutions or establish which, if either, record is Blue Book material.

The supplied evidence identifies one 1968 record matching your question: on November 24, the Atlantic Fleet Weapons Range tracked a high-speed, high-altitude target near Puerto Rico. The record says it rapidly pulled away from a Crusader aircraft flying at Mach 0.99 and 45,000 feet. The fragment’s resolution is recorded as unresolved; the evidence does not identify the target. Its primary narrative is in CIA-UAP-D023.pdf [1968-USN-9E57C2].

The other Puerto Rico record supplied is a Fort Buchanan sighting from 1953, not 1968 [1953-USA-F78A64].

The supplied FBI evidence mentions **Newark Valley, New York**, not a sighting in Newark, New Jersey. In an undated report, farmer Gary Wilcox said he encountered a metallic-like, egg-shaped craft on his dairy farm and spoke with its strangely dressed occupants for about two hours. The archive records his account as unresolved; it does not establish that the craft or occupants were extraterrestrial [UNDATED-FBI-CF55].

The case is the Tremonton, Utah UFO filming of July 2, 1952. Chief Petty Officer Delbert C. Newhouse filmed roughly 30 feet of 16mm color footage of 10–12 unidentified objects near Tremonton; the film fragment’s recorded resolution is unresolved [1952-USN-80203D]. A separate fragment describing Newhouse’s observation at the same place and time is recorded as identified, but the supplied archive lists it under a different canonical event [1952-DOW-141453].

The supplied archive evidence points to these radar cases. These are reported observations, not proof of what the targets were:

- Over the North Sea in January 1947, radar reportedly detected a very rapid object that an RAF Mosquito night fighter tried unsuccessfully to intercept [1947-USN-7828E5].
- On April 18, 1948, an air-search radar tracked a target from about 6,500 to 18,000 yards; the fragment gives an approximate speed of 30 mph but no location [1948-USAF-A09FD8].
- The Fort Monmouth area has two separately recorded cases: a fast-moving radar target on September 10, 1951 [1951-USA-EDD9], and a target near Navesink that appeared nearly stationary on a radar scope before a reported rapid ascent on September 11 [1951-USA-B803].
- In June 1954, the TIMOTHY radar site reported intermittent returns, and an F-86D interceptor obtained an airborne radar pickup that reportedly separated into two returns [1954-USAF-34623D].
- Lakenheath is described in the supplied source as a significant 1956 radar-and-visual case; this fragment does not provide the underlying radar readings [1956-RAF-3BC0B2].
- At Cinq-Mars-la-Pile in France, a radar track was reportedly detected and recorded on January 28, 1994 [1994-USAF-3880AD].

Two further accounts merit qualification: a Washington, D.C., account describes radar returns and dispatched interceptors on July 26, but the supplied case’s date field is undated, so its year is not secure from this evidence [UNDATED-USAF-D173A2]. An undated New Jersey account describes a T-33 chase followed by radar returns; unlike most entries above, its fragment is marked “identified,” without an identification given here [UNDATED-USAF-58C451]. A 1967 claim of radar detection 22,000 miles from Earth is attributed to information received by an anonymous informant, rather than a radar record supplied in the excerpt [1967-FBI-F813AD].

The supplied material includes both Los Alamos-area reports in USAF records and green-fireball observations in DOE-UAP-D004.pdf. The labels do not establish that every Los Alamos report was a Department of Energy report.

In the Los Alamos material, observers reported a greenish-yellow fireball on December 12, 1948, following a nearly horizontal path; a separate December 20 report describes a greenish-white fireball descending and then apparently leveling off, without sound. Both fragments are recorded as unresolved [1948-USAF-DDD5CA] [1948-USAF-BFA2CC]. An undated USAF account also describes multiple reports of greenish-blue fireballs near Los Alamos and elsewhere in New Mexico, said to have flat trajectories and no explosion [UNDATED-USAF-B32231]. Related USAF material records two distinct 1949 Socorro-area reports: no fragments were recovered after searches for the January 30 fireball, while airborne-material collections were made following the July 24 report [1949-USAF-5C0132] [1949-USAF-9D1046].

The DOE-UAP-D004.pdf material includes an undated December 12 discussion contrasting green fireballs with Geminid meteors; the supplied evidence does not establish that it refers to the December 12, 1948 Los Alamos-area event [UNDATED-DOE-80EBE8] [1948-USAF-DDD5CA]. It also contains an August 4 report near Oregon, a Kirtland Field/Arizona account in which observers reported different colors, and an American Meteor Society observation assessed in the record as an ordinary fireball—not an unresolved anomaly [UNDATED-DOE-A60A48] [UNDATED-USAF-6A96A7] [UNDATED-DOE-DA531C].

The archive contains material for two separate October 2023 recordings made by law-enforcement officers in Colorado. One is a transcript of a 1-minute, 19-second video titled LLE-UAP-PR 00J; AARO removed the audio to protect privacy and sensitive information. Its fragment records the UAP as unresolved [UNDATED-LLE-A4576B]. The other is a transcript of a 27-second video titled LLE-UAP-PR003. Its audio contained indistinct background noise but no discernible dialogue, and its fragment also records the UAP as unresolved [UNDATED-LLE-2234ED].

The archive contains a CIA-sourced report about a sighting at Site 7 of the Sary Shagan weapons testing range in late summer 1973. A Soviet citizen reported seeing a bright green circular object or mass in the sky west of the site. The archive summary says it expanded into concentric circles before fading, with no associated sound. The fragment is marked unresolved; it does not establish what the object was [UNDATED-CIA-158652].

In DOW-UAP-D099.pdf, the “Ghost Rockets” are described as a **1946 reporting wave**, not a single incident. The file says the press first reported flying missiles over southern Sweden in late May and gave them that name. Reports followed from Finland and Denmark in June; Swedish sightings increased sharply by July, when reports also came from Norway. Its summary puts the reporting period through October, says Swedish authorities received nearly 1,000 reports, and describes the objects as either “a ball of fire with a tail” or “shiny cigar-shaped objects” [UNDATED-DOW-EA3896].

The same file gives a particular account: on 14 August, a Swedish Air Force pilot reported seeing a dark, cigar-shaped object over central Sweden. Its stated dimensions, distance and speed were observations or estimates in that report, not an established identification [1946-OTHER-78B6E7].

A separate document describes sightings in Swedish skies from February to December 1946, but that broader date range comes from a different source and should not be silently substituted for the chronology in DOW-UAP-D099.pdf [1946-NASA-A146CF]. The supplied excerpts do not establish what the reported ghost rockets were.

No. These records document reported sightings and claims, not proof that extraterrestrials visited Earth. The Nebraska account alleges that an object landed with six people aboard, but the fragment is marked “identified” and does not establish that the people were extraterrestrial [UNDATED-USAF-A8C2]. The claim that “beings from outer space” sought a downed object came from an anonymous informant and remains unresolved [UNDATED-FBI-7A053E-3E85]. Other unresolved reports describe aerial objects or apparent debris, but do not establish extraterrestrial origin [1966-CIA-B2A386].

The supplied archive evidence names **no alien species**. The closest physical description is a witness’s report from Muenster, Germany, of four approximately 3½-foot-tall creatures with thick-set bodies, oversized heads, delicate legs, and rubber-like clothing. The fragment does not establish what they were [UNDATED-FBI-B818DC].

Other records refer to alleged occupants, “beings from outer space,” or alleged alien corpses without identifying a species [UNDATED-USAF-A8C2] [UNDATED-FBI-CF55] [UNDATED-FBI-7A053E-3E85] [2023-DEPARTMENT-98C959].

None of the supplied records establishes that a UAP used anti-gravity. They describe observations—including reported sharp turns and rapid movement—but do not identify an anti-gravity mechanism [2023-USAF-73C2E4] [UNDATED-USAF-668927].

None of the supplied government records proves that alien bodies were recovered. An FBI record reports a claim that a disc in the Mojave Desert contained eighteen dead, human-like occupants; it does not establish that the disc or occupants existed [UNDATED-FBI-8002]. A Roswell-related account says Colonel Corso reportedly saw a preserved occupant, but that, too, is a claim rather than verified evidence of a recovered body [1947-USAF-A120D8].

The supplied evidence does not identify who piloted the spacecraft. In Truman Bethurum’s account, a female commandant allegedly supervised a crew of assumed space explorers, but the record does not say she was the pilot [UNDATED-FBI-3A8615].

None of the supplied cases conclusively proves non-human technology. The Roswell fragment recounts Colonel Corso’s claim that the recovered object was extraterrestrial, but records the case as unresolved; his claim is not a conclusive finding [1947-USAF-A120D8].

The supplied archive evidence does not identify a secret treaty with an alien government. It includes a secondhand story about two men who supposedly claimed to be from Venus, but that account says nothing about a treaty [UNDATED-FBI-D50072].

None of the supplied records confirms a weaponized UFO. In the Belgium account, the F-16s—not the UFO—were armed with missiles [UNDATED-NASA-801C9E]. In the Iraq account, a military aircraft released a weapon before its crew observed an unidentified object; the record does not say the object was armed [2024-USAF-3A06FB].

The supplied records do not identify or locate an extraterrestrial base. They describe reported sightings and claims, including one anonymous informant’s claim about “beings from outer space,” but give no location for a base [UNDATED-FBI-7A053E-3E85].

None of the supplied incidents proves a crash retrieval of a flying saucer. The Roswell record says military personnel recovered debris after the base initially announced a crashed “flying disk,” but it also says the base retracted that description and called the object a weather balloon [1947-USAF-2C9F14]. The Coulter account is a secondhand claim that two recovered saucers were seen at a radar station; the fragment is unresolved, not a verified retrieval [UNDATED-FBI-AC2C].
